newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo investors return from holiday in buying mood.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo investors return from holiday in buying mood.

text.p: Tokyo investors couldn't wait to get back to business on Tuesday after a long weekend, sending the key Nikkei stock average up by more than two percent, on the back of Wall Street's record climb in overnight trade.

"The strong U.S. markets -- both the Dow and the Nikkei futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange -- influenced the Tokyo markets strongly today," said Haruo Nakaharu, a strategist at Toyo Securities.
"The Nikkei average had some catching up to do, since Monday was a holiday in Japan," he said.
The benchmark Nikkei 225 closed 2.25 percent or 467.95 points higher at 21,310.59, after briefly recording 500 point gains in the afternoon session.
Brokers said market sentiment had brightened considerably after the settlement on Friday of Nikkei 225 futures and options, or "special quotations" (SQ).
Contrary to market worries, the settlement ended on Friday morning with more buy positions than sell positions, lifting the market for the remainder of the session.
"Basically, there's a feeling of relief now in the market that the SQ ended without an upheaval," said Ryoichi Ohta, a general manager at Tokyo Securities.
Brokers added that Wall Street's recent strength was a sign that interest rate rises were not imminent and that was in turn encouraging the Nikkei average.
On Monday, the Dow Industrials jumped to a record close for a second successive session, surging 51 points to about 5,889.
Brokers said, however, that apart from bullishness overseas there were few factors to drive the Nikkei average.
"The Nikkei average is strong but trade is mostly arbitrage-linked or brokers buying and selling their own positions, and interest is focused solely on major issues," said Tokyo Securities' Ohta.
Arbitrageurs simultaneously trade stocks and their underlying futures, and profit from momentary discrepancies between the prices of the two instruments.
"The market has found a firm footing now, but reassurance that it is not going to crash past the 20,000 line is not a factor to prompt investors to keep buying," Ohta said.
Foreign investors were stepping up their buying of Japanese stocks and brokers hoped that would help activate the market and boost turnover.
Turnover in the first section was 423 million shares, down from an expiry-inflated 705 million on Friday.
